rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Which executes first — UI Policy or Client Script? When to use which?
rows.answerText:
UI Policy executes before Client Scripts on form load. Execution order: UI Policies (onLoad) → Client Scripts (onLoad). For field changes, UI Policy actions apply first, then onChange Client Scripts fire.

When to use UI Policy — for simple, no-code form behavior: making fields mandatory, read-only, or visible based on straightforward conditions. Faster to configure and easier to maintain for non-developers.

When to use Client Script — when complex logic is needed: conditional checks, GlideAjax calls, dynamic calculations, or behavior that UI Policy conditions cannot express. Also when you need to manipulate multiple fields or show custom messages based on logic.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: incident.none → itil, incident.* → itil_admin, incident.priority → admin. If itil_admin logs in, what can they edit and why?
rows.answerText:
An itil_admin user has the itil_admin role. ACL evaluation combines a row-level ACL with field-level ACLs, and a user must pass both to read/write a given field:

incident.none (itil) — the row-level ACL requires the itil role. Since itil_admin is commonly configured to extend/inherit the itil role, this user passes the row-level check and can access the record.
incident.* (itil_admin) — this field-level ACL (wildcard, applying to all fields not covered by a more specific field ACL) requires the itil_admin role, which this user has, so they can read and write those fields.
incident.priority (admin) — this specific field-level ACL on the priority field requires the admin role. The user does not have that role, so they cannot edit priority specifically, even though they passed the row-level and general field-level checks.

Result: itil_admin can view and edit all fields on the Incident record except priority, which is restricted to the admin role only.

rows.title: Difference between =, ==, and ===.
rows.answerText:
= — assignment operator. Assigns a value to a variable. var x = 5;
== — loose equality. Compares values after type coercion. '5' == 5 returns true.
=== — strict equality. Compares both value and type without coercion. '5' === 5 returns false.

Always prefer === in scripts to avoid unexpected behavior from type coercion.

rows.title: What is Turnstile activity in Workflow?
rows.answerText: A Turnstile activity in a Workflow synchronizes parallel branches. It holds execution at that point until every parallel branch that was running simultaneously has completed. Once all branches finish, the workflow proceeds past the turnstile to the next activity — this prevents the workflow from continuing prematurely while some branches are still in progress.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What are ACLs? Difference between * and none.
rows.answerText: table.none is a row-level (record-level) ACL: if a user fails it, they cannot see or access the record at all, regardless of which fields they are trying to read or write. table.* is a field-level ACL using the wildcard field name: it controls access to all fields on the table (or, when a specific field name is used instead of *, to just that one field). A user can pass a row-level ACL and still be blocked from specific fields by a field-level ACL — row-level and field-level checks are evaluated independently, and both must pass for a field to be visible/editable.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Reporting & Database Views
rows.title: Have you worked on Reports and Database Views?
rows.answerText: Yes. Reports are created under Reports → Create New for list, bar, pie, trend, and pivot types. For data spanning multiple tables, a Database View is created under System Definition → Database Views by joining tables on a common key. The view acts as a virtual table and can be used as a report data source, enabling cross-table reporting without custom development.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Notifications & Events
rows.title: How are Notifications managed?
rows.answerText: Notifications are managed under System Notification → Notifications. Each notification has a target table, trigger conditions (insert/update/event), recipient definition (users, groups, roles, or dynamic fields), email template (subject and body using variables), and a device/channel (email, SMS). Notifications can also use Notification Digest to batch emails and Weight to handle conflicts. They can be triggered by events using gs.eventQueue().

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: What is an Order Guide?
rows.answerText: An Order Guide is a catalog item that bundles multiple catalog items together into a single submission. When a user fills out the Order Guide, all included catalog items are submitted as separate RITMs under one REQ. The Cascade Variables checkbox passes Order Guide-level variable values down to the individual catalog items automatically, reducing redundant data entry.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: Have you worked on Catalog Items? Explain requirements and challenges.
rows.answerText: Yes. A common requirement was creating a New Hire onboarding catalog item with variables for personal details, equipment selection, and system access. The flow created SCTASKs for IT, HR, and Facilities simultaneously. A challenge was populating manager and department details dynamically based on the requested-for user, which was solved using GlideAjax with a Script Include. Another challenge was restricting certain catalog item variables based on the user's department, handled using scoped client scripts on the catalog item.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: Difference between Normal and Emergency Change.
rows.answerText:
Normal Change: a Normal Change is planned, reviewed, and executed through the full change process. It goes through CAB approval and risk assessment, and is scheduled within an approved maintenance window. It is used for regular updates, enhancements, and planned releases, with the goal of controlled, low-risk execution.

Emergency Change: an Emergency Change is raised when a critical issue needs to be fixed immediately and there isn't time for the normal approval cycle. It uses an expedited approval path (CAB-EC), is implemented with minimal planning, and requires a mandatory Post Implementation Review (PIR) afterward. It is used for production outages and other critical fixes, where the goal is to restore service quickly and formally review the change after the fact.

In short: Normal changes are planned and controlled; Emergency changes are urgent and reactive.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: Types of Change in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText:
ServiceNow supports three standard change types:

- Standard Change — pre-approved, low-risk, routine changes (for example, a password reset). No CAB approval is required because the change has been vetted and templated in advance.
- Normal Change — planned changes that go through full CAB (Change Advisory Board) review, risk assessment, and approval before implementation.
- Emergency Change — urgent changes needed to resolve a critical issue; approved through an expedited CAB-EC (Emergency CAB) process, implemented with minimal delay, and followed by a mandatory Post Implementation Review (PIR).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: Have you worked on Data Sources and Import Sets?
rows.answerText: Yes. A Data Source defines where the import data comes from — file (Excel/CSV), JDBC, LDAP, REST, or FTP. An Import Set is the staging table where raw data lands before transformation. A Transform Map then maps and moves data from the import set to the target table. Scheduled imports can automate this process end to end without manual uploads.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Notifications & Events
rows.title: On Notification, what is "Weight" and its use?
rows.answerText: Weight on a notification determines priority when multiple notifications are triggered for the same record at the same time. The notification with the higher weight value takes precedence and is sent, while lower-weight notifications for the same record may be suppressed. This prevents users from receiving duplicate or redundant emails when multiple conditions are met simultaneously.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: Difference between Approval Groups and Approval Users.
rows.answerText: Approval Users — specific named users are set as approvers; each user gets an individual approval record and must approve/reject individually. Approval Groups — a group is set as the approver; ServiceNow creates approval records for each member of the group or uses the group-level approval rule (anyone approves vs everyone approves). Approval Groups are more flexible and maintainable since membership changes don't require workflow modifications.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Workflow Activities

rows.questionText: Use Workflow Scratchpad — a shared data store within a workflow execution that all activities can read from and write to.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Make Short Description mandatory for a particular view only.
rows.answerText: Create a UI Policy scoped to the specific view (set the View field on the UI Policy to the target view). Add the condition and set Short Description as mandatory in the UI Policy Action. Since the UI Policy is view-specific, it only applies when the form is opened in that view. Do NOT set it mandatory in the dictionary, as that would apply globally across all views.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Difference between UI Policy and Data Policy.
rows.answerText:
UI Policy (client-side behavior): a UI Policy runs in the browser on the form the user is interacting with. It controls form behavior — showing or hiding fields, making fields mandatory or read-only, and reacting instantly when a user changes a value. Because it runs client-side, it is fast and interactive, but it can be bypassed by anything that doesn't load the form, such as the API, import sets, background scripts, or list edit. Use a UI Policy when you want to control what the user sees and how the form behaves, and you need immediate feedback — but keep in mind it only governs the UI, not the underlying data.

Data Policy (server-side enforcement): a Data Policy enforces rules at the server/database level, independent of the UI. It ensures mandatory fields are filled and rules are applied no matter how the data is entered — through the UI, API, import, or integration. Because it runs server-side, it cannot be bypassed the way a UI Policy can. Use a Data Policy when you need strict, channel-independent enforcement of data integrity rules.

Core difference: a UI Policy controls how users interact with the form; a Data Policy controls what data is allowed into the system regardless of entry point.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: What is a UI Policy?
rows.answerText: A UI Policy is a client-side rule that dynamically controls form behavior based on conditions — without writing JavaScript. It can make fields mandatory, read-only, or visible/hidden when defined conditions are true. It runs in the browser when the form loads or when a referenced field changes. UI Policy Actions define what happens to specific fields when the condition is met.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Types of Client Scripts and use of isTemplate in onChange.
rows.questionText:
Types: onLoad (fires when form loads), onChange (fires when a specific field value changes), onSubmit (fires when form is submitted), onCellEdit (fires when a cell is edited in list view).
isTemplate in onChange — this parameter is true when the field value is being set by a template (not by the user manually). Using if (isTemplate) return; prevents the onChange logic from firing when a template populates the field, avoiding unintended side effects.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scheduled Jobs & Background Scripts
rows.title: What is a Fix Script?
rows.answerText: A Fix Script is a one-time server-side script stored in the database and tracked in update sets. It is used to perform data fixes, migrations, or one-time operations that need to be promoted across instances (Dev → QA → Prod). Unlike Background Scripts, Fix Scripts are stored, auditable, and can be version-controlled. After execution, they should be marked as run to avoid re-execution.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Best practices while creating Business Rules?
rows.answerText:
1 - Use specific When conditions (insert/update/delete) and field conditions to limit execution scope.
2 - Prefer Async for background tasks — never block the form unnecessarily.
3 - Never call current.update() in After or Async BRs.
4 - Use setWorkflow(false) when updating related records inside a BR.
5 - Move reusable logic to Script Includes to keep BR scripts clean and short.
6 - Always test with ACL debug and impersonation before promoting to production.
7 - Add comments explaining the business purpose of the BR.

rows.title: What is getMethod() and how to use it in a Business Rule?

rows.title: Use of GlideAggregate?
rows.questionText: GlideAggregate is used to perform aggregate database operations like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX without fetching all records — much more efficient than looping through GlideRecord results.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Workflow Activities
rows.title: Use of setWorkflow() and difference between _next() and next().
rows.questionText:
setWorkflow(false) — suppresses Business Rules, workflows, and other automation when updating a record programmatically. Used in batch updates to avoid unintended side effects.

next() — moves to the next record in the result set AND enforces ACL checks. If the user doesn't have access to a record, it is skipped.
_next() — moves to the next record bypassing ACL checks. Used in system-level scripts where you need all records regardless of user permissions.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > GlideRecord & GlideAggregate
rows.title: Difference between GlideRecord and GlideRecordSecure.
rows.questionText: GlideRecord — standard server-side API to query and manipulate records. It bypasses ACL checks — even if a field or record is restricted, GlideRecord can still read and write it. GlideRecordSecure — respects ACL rules during query and field access. If the running user doesn't have access to a field or record, GlideRecordSecure will not return it. Use GlideRecordSecure when you want to enforce security rules within a script — for example in a Scripted REST API exposed to end users.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How is After Business Rule different from Async?
rows.answerText:
After Business Rule (synchronous): an After Business Rule runs immediately after the record is saved to the database, but still within the same transaction. The platform waits for it to complete before the transaction is considered done, so any logic here is part of the same unit of work — if it fails, the transaction can be affected. Use an After Business Rule when you need guaranteed data consistency, such as updating related records that must stay in sync with the record that was just saved, and when the logic depends on the current record being fully committed. Because it runs inline, heavy logic here will slow down the form save for the user, so it should be kept lightweight.

Async Business Rule (asynchronous): an Async Business Rule runs after the triggering transaction has completed, picked up separately by a scheduled/background job (the async processor). The user's form save does not wait for it, so it is decoupled from the user's action, and it does not guarantee exact timing or ordering relative to other events. Use an Async Business Rule when the outcome doesn't need to be immediate and the work can happen in the background — for example, notifications, integrations, or logging — where performance and responsiveness for the end user matter more than immediacy. Because it runs independently and later, the underlying data may have changed by the time it executes, so it should not assume the record is in exactly the same state as when it was triggered.

Both types should avoid calling current.update() inside them, since that re-triggers Business Rules on the same record and can cause recursion or a performance hit.

Rule of thumb for interviews: After Business Rule prioritizes consistency; Async Business Rule prioritizes performance and decoupling.

rows.title: What is the use of onForeignInsert() script in a Transform Map?
rows.answerText: onForeignInsert() is a Transform Map event script that runs when a coalesce match is not found and a new record needs to be inserted into a related (foreign) table during transformation. It is used when a field in the import data references a record in another table that doesn't exist yet — instead of failing, onForeignInsert() handles the creation of that missing related record before the main transformation continues. For example, if a department name in the import doesn't exist in the Department table, onForeignInsert() can create it automatically.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > GlideRecord & GlideAggregate
rows.title: What is addJoinQuery in GlideRecord? Where should we use it?
rows.questionText: addJoinQuery() allows you to filter records from one table based on the existence (or non-existence) of related records in another table — similar to a SQL JOIN. Use it when you need to find records in Table A that have or don't have matching records in Table B.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > Reference Qualifiers
rows.title: Reference qualifier — difference between Dynamic and Advanced.
rows.questionText: A Reference Qualifier filters the records available in a reference field lookup. Dynamic — uses a predefined dynamic filter key (like dynamic_ref_qual) stored in a script, selectable from a dropdown, reusable across multiple fields without rewriting. Advanced — allows writing a custom encoded query or script directly on the field for one-off, specific filtering needs. Dynamic is preferred for reusability; Advanced is used when the filter logic is unique to that field.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: Difference between Variables and Variable Set.
rows.answerText: A Variable is a single input field (text, choice, reference, etc.) created directly on one specific catalog item — it belongs only to that item. A Variable Set is a reusable, named collection of variables that can be attached to multiple catalog items at once, so a common set of fields doesn't have to be recreated on every item — this avoids duplication and keeps those shared fields consistent across all the items that use the set.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Reporting & Database Views
rows.title: How to create a single report from multiple tables?
rows.answerText: Use a Report based on a Database View or use the Report type: List/Bar with a joined table. The proper approach is to create a Database View (under System Definition → Database Views) that joins the required tables using common fields. Once the view is created, create a report on that view as if it were a single table. This allows data from multiple tables to appear in one unified report without duplication.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Workflow Activities
rows.title: Some workflow activities and their explanation.
rows.answerText:
1 - Approval — sends an approval request to a user or group; flow proceeds based on approve/reject outcome.
2 - Notification — sends an email or in-app notification to specified recipients at that point in the workflow.
3 - Run Script — executes a custom server-side script within the workflow context, allowing GlideRecord operations.
4 - Set Values — sets field values on the current record without scripting — a no-code activity.
5 - Wait for Condition — pauses the workflow until a defined condition on the record becomes true.
6 - Turnstile — synchronizes parallel branches; waits for all parallel paths to complete before continuing.
7 - Timer — pauses the workflow for a defined duration before proceeding to the next activity.
8 - Rollback — used in Change workflows to revert implementation steps if something fails.

rows.title: Which Business Rule types should not include current.update() and why?
rows.answerText: After and Async Business Rules should never use current.update(). In an After BR, the record is already saved — calling current.update() triggers another save, which re-fires Business Rules, potentially causing infinite loops. In Async BRs, the transaction is already complete, and current.update() similarly causes unintended re-triggers. In Before BRs, changes to current are automatically saved with the original transaction — so current.update() is also unnecessary there.

rows.title: Which executes first — Client Script or UI Policy?
rows.answerText: UI Policies execute before Client Scripts on form load. The execution order on load is: UI Policies (onLoad) → Client Scripts (onLoad). For field changes, UI Policy actions apply first, then onChange Client Scripts fire. However, this order can sometimes vary by instance version, so it's best not to create dependencies between the two.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: What is Retroactive Start and Pause in SLA?
rows.answerText: Retroactive Start means the SLA timer starts from when the record was first created, not from when the SLA condition was met. So even if the SLA was attached later, the timer backdates to creation time. Retroactive Pause means any pause durations are calculated from the record's creation time, subtracting all periods when the ticket was in a paused state — even those that occurred before the SLA attached.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: Difference between Query Business Rules and ACL.
rows.answerText: A Query Business Rule runs when a list or query is executed and uses addQuery() or addEncodedQuery() on current to filter which records are returned — it controls what data the user sees at the query level. An ACL controls access at the record or field level based on roles, conditions, and scripts — it either grants or denies access to a specific record or field. Query BRs filter results silently; ACLs block access explicitly and can return errors.

rows.title: Best practices for Business Rules?

1 - Always use specific conditions on the BR to limit when it runs — avoid running on every insert/update.
2 - Use Async for non-critical background operations to avoid holding the form.
3 - Never use current.update() in After or Async BRs — it causes recursion.
4 - Use setWorkflow(false) when updating related records inside a BR to avoid triggering a chain of rules.
5 - Move reusable logic into Script Includes instead of embedding everything in the BR script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Can we execute an onChange Client Script during form load? How?
rows.questionText: By default, onChange does not fire on load. To run onChange logic on load, manually call the shared function from an onLoad Client Script:

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: When an Incident goes to Resolved state, make all fields read-only except Additional Comments. How?
rows.questionText:
Use a UI Policy with the condition State is Resolved. In the UI Policy actions, set all fields to Read Only = true. Add a specific action for additional_comments and set it to Read Only = false. This ensures all fields lock except the comments field when the incident is resolved.
For server-side enforcement, use a Before Update Business Rule to prevent field changes:

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: Have you worked on Inbound Actions?
rows.answerText: Yes. Inbound Email Actions process incoming emails to ServiceNow. Based on conditions like subject, body, or sender, they can create, update, or reply to records. For example, when a customer replies to an incident email, the inbound action matches the watermark in the email to the incident and adds the reply as a comment automatically. They are configured under System Policy → Email → Inbound Actions.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: Excel with 10 columns — first 5 to Hardware table, last 5 to Software table — single upload. How?
rows.answerText: Create a single Import Set by uploading the Excel. Then create two Transform Maps — one mapping columns 1–5 to the Hardware table and another mapping columns 6–10 to the Software table — both pointing to the same import set table. When the import runs, both transform maps execute against the same staged data, populating both target tables from a single upload.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: Catalog Item with requester field — auto-populate details using GlideAjax.
rows.questionText: (Similar to question 043 but within catalog item context — use an onChange client script on the requester variable.)

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: Five best practices for server-side scripting.
rows.answerText:
1 - Use setWorkflow(false) and autoSysFields(false) when doing bulk updates to avoid triggering unintended business rules.
2- Always use addQuery() before query() — never iterate the full table without filters to avoid performance issues.
3- Avoid current.update() in After and Async Business Rules to prevent recursive triggers.
4 - Use Script Includes for reusable logic instead of duplicating code across multiple Business Rules.
5 - Use gs.info() or gs.error() for logging instead of hardcoded alerts; always remove debug logs before moving to production.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Notifications & Events
rows.title: Catalog Item with Manager Approval — send reminder notifications on Day 3, 6, 9 until approved/rejected. How?
rows.questionText:
Use a Scheduled Job combined with a query on pending approvals, or use SLA with notifications on the approval record. The cleanest approach is using Flow Designer with a Wait for Condition loop and a scheduled delay:
In Flow Designer:

Trigger on RITM creation.
Add Ask for Approval step.
Before it, add a Do the following until loop checking approval state.
Inside the loop, add a Wait action for 3 days, then a Send Notification action to the manager.
Loop exits when approval state becomes Approved or Rejected.
