rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: On an Incident form with a related list of Incident Tasks, hide the "Edit" button when the Incident is assigned to the "Hardware" group. How?
rows.questionText: Use a List Control or a UI Policy on the related list combined with a client script. Since UI Policies don't directly control related list buttons, use an onLoad/onChange Client Script with g_list or use a Formatter approach. The most reliable way is a UI Action with a visibility condition, or hiding via a client script:

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > User Criteria & Data Visibility
rows.title: I want a catalog item to be seen only by members of a database group. How?
rows.answerText: Use User Criteria. Create a User Criteria record under Service Catalog → User Criteria and set the condition to match the specific group. Then attach this User Criteria to the catalog item under the "Available For" section. Only users who are members of that group will see the catalog item in the portal or service catalog.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: What is the use of "Inherit" and "Global" checkbox in a Client Script?
rows.answerText: Inherit — when checked, the client script applies to the current table and all tables that extend it. For example, a client script on the Task table with Inherit checked will also run on Incident, Problem, and Change since they extend Task. Global — when checked, the client script runs across all views of the form. If unchecked, it only runs in the specific view it was configured for.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: What is the use of "On Load" and "Reverse if False" in a UI Policy?
rows.answerText: On Load — when checked, the UI Policy evaluates and applies its actions as soon as the form loads, not just when a field changes. Reverse if False — when the UI Policy condition becomes false, the actions are automatically reversed. For example, if a field was made mandatory when condition was true, it becomes non-mandatory when the condition turns false — without needing a separate UI Policy for the reverse.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: When does a UI Policy execute?
rows.answerText: A UI Policy executes in three scenarios: when the form loads (if "On Load" is checked), when the value of a field changes that is referenced in the UI Policy condition, and when any field on the form changes if no specific field condition is set. It runs entirely on the client side in the browser.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: How can we create a knowledge article from an incident as an out-of-the-box feature?
rows.answerText: On the Incident form, there is a "Create Knowledge" button available in the related links or form buttons section (depending on the instance version). Clicking it pre-populates a Knowledge article with the incident's short description and resolution notes. This is an OOTB feature under Knowledge Management and requires the Knowledge plugin to be active. The article goes into Draft state and follows the Knowledge workflow for review and publishing.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: Same Variable Set in two catalog items but show only 5 of 10 choices in one. How?
rows.questionText: Use a Client Script scoped to the specific catalog item to hide or remove unwanted choices dynamically on that item's form, while leaving the variable set unchanged.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: What is the difference between a Variable and a Variable Set?
rows.answerText: A Variable is a single input field (text, choice, reference, etc.) created directly on a specific catalog item — it belongs to that item only. A Variable Set is a reusable collection of variables grouped together that can be attached to multiple catalog items, avoiding duplication and ensuring consistency across items that share common fields.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: How do you configure a Catalog Item?
rows.answerText: Navigate to Service Catalog → Catalog Definitions → Maintain Items. Create a new item, set the name, category, icon, and short description. Add Variables or Variable Sets for user input fields. Configure the Process Engine (Flow or Workflow) for fulfillment. Set Availability using User Criteria. Define Pricing if applicable. Add Knowledge articles for self-service guidance. Test via the Service Portal before publishing.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > General & Behavioral > Experience & Background
rows.title: What kind of work have you done in ITSM?
rows.answerText: Worked across Incident, Problem, Change, and Service Catalog modules — configuring SLA definitions, assignment rules, approval flows, Business Rules for automation, ACLs for security, notifications, and catalog items with flows for fulfillment. Also worked on CMDB basics, Knowledge Management, and reporting dashboards for SLA performance tracking.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What work have you done in Integration? Scripted REST API? Difference between PATCH and PUT? Data format?
rows.answerText: In integrations, I have worked on outbound REST integrations using RESTMessageV2 and inbound integrations using Scripted REST APIs. A Scripted REST API is a custom API built in ServiceNow where we define our own endpoints, HTTP methods, and response logic — used when Table API is insufficient. PUT replaces the entire record with the provided payload, while PATCH updates only the specified fields leaving others unchanged. Data was exchanged in JSON format in most integrations, with some legacy systems using XML/SOAP.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: When all active Problems linked to Incidents are resolved, auto-resolve those Incidents.
rows.questionText: Use an Async Business Rule on the problem table that triggers on update when state changes to Resolved.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Notifications & Events
rows.title: Trigger a notification when a Knowledge article moves from Draft to Published.
rows.answerText: Create a Notification under System Notification → Notifications on the kb_knowledge table. Set the condition to current.workflow_state == 'published' && previous.workflow_state == 'draft'. Set the recipient to the Author field of the knowledge record. No Business Rule is needed — the notification's built-in record condition handles the trigger directly.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Auto-populate Description with Short Description and logged-in user's name on Incident submission. How?
rows.questionText: Use an onSubmit or onChange Client Script on the short_description field, or an onLoad + onSubmit combination.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: I want two users from a group to approve the RITM. How to configure this?
rows.answerText: In the Flow Designer flow for the catalog item, add an Ask for Approval action on the RITM. Set the approver source to the specific group and set the approval rule to "Everyone must approve" with a count of 2, or use "Percentage" logic. Alternatively, add two separate Ask for Approval steps in sequence — one for each required approver — so both must approve before the flow proceeds.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Show the logged-in user's manager name in a field without scripting. How?
rows.answerText: Use a dot-walked default value on the field. On the form, set the field's default value using the variable javascript: gs.getUser().getManagerID() or configure a Data Lookup Rule that references the current user's manager. Alternatively, use a Reference field pointing to sys_user and set its default using the built-in variable javascript:gs.getUserID() then dot-walk to manager via a Calculated field with the formula referencing sys_user.manager — no client script needed.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Update Sets & Deployment
rows.title: We have lots of update sets. How to move them from QA to Prod efficiently?
rows.answerText: Use a Batch Update Set. In QA, navigate to System Update Sets → Batch Update Sets, create a new batch, and add all individual update sets to it. Preview the batch in Prod to check for conflicts, resolve any issues, then commit the batch — this applies all update sets in the correct order in a single operation rather than committing them one by one.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How can we restrict a user from submitting a form without an attachment?
rows.questionText: Use an onSubmit Client Script to check if an attachment exists using GlideAjax, and block submission if none found. For server-side enforcement, use a Before Business Rule.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: A field "type" determines record creation — Incident if "Incident", Problem if "Problem". How to achieve this?
rows.questionText: Use an Async Business Rule on the source table triggered on insert/update when the type field changes.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: For a catalog item, I want approval on the Request. Can we do this? If yes, how?
rows.answerText: Yes. In the catalog item's Process Engine tab, attach a Flow or Workflow that includes an approval step at the REQ level. In Flow Designer, use the Ask for Approval action targeting the sc_request table. Alternatively, use the Catalog Item → Approval section to configure approvers directly. The flow triggers on RITM creation and can request approval on the parent REQ record.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: What is the difference between a Request, RITM, and a Catalog Task?
rows.answerText:
Request (REQ) — the top-level order record created when a user submits one or more catalog items. Acts as the container.
Request Item (RITM) — created for each individual catalog item within the request. Tracks the fulfillment of that specific item including its variables.
Catalog Task (SCTASK) — created under an RITM for individual fulfillment steps assigned to different teams. One RITM can have multiple SCTASKs.

Example: Ordering a laptop and software in one cart = one REQ, two RITMs, and each RITM may have multiple SCTASKs for procurement, imaging, and delivery.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: Where do we use on-demand Script Includes?
rows.answerText: On-demand Script Includes are used when we want to encapsulate reusable server-side logic that is called explicitly — from Business Rules, Scheduled Jobs, other Script Includes, REST API scripts, or Transform Maps. They do not execute automatically and only run when invoked, promoting code reuse and separation of concerns.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: How many types of Script Includes are there?
rows.answerText:
There are two types:

On-demand (standard) — a regular class-based or function-based Script Include called explicitly from other server-side scripts or GlideAjax.
Client Callable — has the "Client callable" checkbox enabled, allowing it to be called from client-side scripts via GlideAjax. It must extend AbstractAjaxProcessor.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: For a reference field value, which is better — getReference() or GlideAjax?
rows.questionText: GlideAjax is better. getReference() is a synchronous call that blocks the browser until the server responds, degrading UI performance. GlideAjax is asynchronous and non-blocking. ServiceNow officially discourages getReference() in favor of GlideAjax for fetching reference field data.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: In how many ways can we call a server-side script from the client side?
rows.answerText:
Three ways:

GlideAjax — calls a Client Callable Script Include asynchronously from a client script.
g_scratchpad — Display Business Rule passes server-side data to client scripts at form load via g_scratchpad.
Scripted REST API + XMLHttpRequest / fetch — advanced approach where client-side code calls a custom REST endpoint. Rarely used in standard form scripting but applicable in Service Portal widgets using spUtil.get() or spUtil.post().

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: On a UI Policy, there is a Global checkbox — what does it do?
rows.answerText: The Global checkbox on a UI Policy means the policy applies to all views of that form, not just the current view it was created in. If unchecked, the UI Policy only executes when the record is viewed in the specific form view it was configured for. Checking Global ensures consistent behavior across all views including popups and mobile.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Can we trigger an onChange Client Script on load?
rows.questionText: Yes. By default, onChange does not fire on load. But if we set the isLoading parameter check to false or ignore it, and set the client script's "Run on load" option (available in some versions), it can fire on load. Alternatively, we handle load-time logic in an onLoad client script separately. However, if we want onChange to intentionally run on load, we can call the function manually from an onLoad script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: How many types of scripts are there in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText:
ServiceNow scripts are broadly categorized as:

Client-side: Client Scripts, UI Policies (with scripts), UI Actions (client-side)
Server-side: Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, Fix Scripts, Background Scripts, UI Actions (server-side), Inbound Email Actions, SLA Scripts
Flow/Automation: Flow Designer scripts, Workflow scripts, Action scripts in IntegrationHub
Integration: REST Message scripts, Scripted REST APIs, Transform Map scripts (onBefore, onAfter, onComplete)

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: What are the types of inbound email actions?
rows.answerText: Inbound Email Actions define what happens when ServiceNow receives an email. The types based on their action are: Create (creates a new record when an email is received), Update (updates an existing record by matching the email's watermark or subject to a record), and Reply (adds the email content as a work note or comment to an existing record). They are configured under System Policy → Email → Inbound Actions.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Can we trigger a notification through a Business Rule?
rows.answerText: Yes. In a Business Rule, we can use gs.eventQueue('event.name', current, param1, param2) to fire an event that is mapped to a notification. Alternatively, we can use the notification's built-in conditions to match the Business Rule trigger scenario, or directly use gs.sendNotificationEmail('notification_name', current) within the script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Notifications & Events
rows.title: What are the ways to trigger a notification? Can we trigger one through a scheduled job?
rows.answerText: Notifications can be triggered via: Notification records (event-based or record insert/update conditions), Business Rules using gs.eventQueue() to fire an event that triggers a notification, Flow Designer using the Send Notification action, and Script using gs.sendNotificationEmail(). Yes, a scheduled job can trigger a notification by queuing an event or directly calling the notification API within its script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: What is the approval coordinator and what kind of approvals can we add in it?
rows.answerText: The Approval Coordinator in Workflow is an activity that manages multiple approval requests in parallel or sequence. It supports three approval types: Anyone Approves (one approval is sufficient), Everyone Must Approve (all approvers must approve), and Percentage Approves (a defined percentage of approvers must approve before the flow proceeds).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Workflow Activities
rows.title: What is a rollback activity in Workflow?
rows.answerText: A Rollback activity in Workflow is used in Change Management workflows to revert a change if implementation fails. It triggers a predefined set of rollback steps, setting the change state to indicate rollback is in progress, and allows teams to restore the system to its prior state in a controlled manner.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Workflow Activities
rows.title: What is a turnstile activity in Workflow?
rows.answerText: A Turnstile activity in Workflow is used to synchronize parallel branches. It holds the workflow at that point until all parallel branches that were running simultaneously have completed. Once all branches finish, the workflow proceeds past the turnstile to the next activity.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: What is the use of a spoke in Flow Designer?
rows.answerText: A spoke is a scoped application in IntegrationHub that provides pre-built actions for integrating with external systems — such as Jira, Slack, ServiceNow itself, or Microsoft Teams. Instead of writing custom REST calls, you use a spoke's actions directly inside a flow to interact with third-party platforms.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: What is the use of data pills in a flow?
rows.answerText: Data pills represent field values from a trigger record or a previous step's output. They allow you to pass and reference data dynamically across all steps in a flow without hardcoding values. For example, a data pill from the trigger can carry the incident's caller or priority into an approval step or notification.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: What are the trigger types in Flow Designer?
rows.answerText: The main trigger types are: Record-based (when a record is created, updated, or deleted), Schedule-based (runs at a defined time or interval), Inbound Email (triggered by an incoming email), Application (triggered by a ServiceNow application like HR or CSM), and Subflow (triggered when called from another flow).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: Have you worked on flows?
rows.answerText: Yes. Flow Designer is a low-code automation tool used to build process flows triggered by record events, schedules, or inbound actions. It uses a visual interface with actions, conditions, and data pills. It replaces traditional Workflows for most use cases and integrates natively with IntegrationHub spokes.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: You are updating Assignment Group for X incidents via background script and don't want to trigger existing Business Rules. How?
rows.questionText: Use GlideRecord.autoSysFields(false) and GlideRecord.setWorkflow(false) to suppress business rules and workflow execution during the update.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: What does the gsft function do?
rows.answerText: gsft refers to the ServiceNow client-side JavaScript framework functions used internally by the platform to manage form behavior. Developers generally do not use gsft functions directly — instead, the g_form, g_user, and g_list APIs are the supported interfaces. Direct use of gsft is discouraged as it may break during upgrades.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: What is an on-demand Script Include?
rows.answerText: A Script Include marked as "Client Callable" that can also be invoked on demand from other server-side scripts, Business Rules, or GlideAjax calls as needed — rather than being tied to a scheduled or automatic trigger. It executes only when explicitly called, making it reusable across multiple contexts.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scheduled Jobs & Background Scripts
rows.title: What is an on-demand scheduled job?
rows.answerText: An on-demand scheduled job is a scheduled job that does not run on a fixed schedule but is triggered manually by a user or programmatically via script using SncTriggerSynchronizer.executeNow(gr). It is useful for one-time executions or testing without waiting for the next scheduled run.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scheduled Jobs & Background Scripts
rows.title: Have you worked on scheduled jobs?
rows.answerText: Yes. Scheduled Jobs are server-side scripts that run automatically at defined intervals — daily, weekly, or on a custom schedule. They are used for tasks like sending reminder notifications, archiving old records, syncing data, or running batch operations. They are configured under System Definition → Scheduled Jobs.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: Have you worked on ACL? Types? Difference between table.none and table.*?
rows.answerText: Yes. ACL types are Table-level and Field-level. table.None (row-level) controls access to the entire record — if a user fails this ACL, they cannot see the record at all. table.* (field-level, using * or a specific field name) controls access to individual fields on a record. A user may pass the row-level ACL but still be denied specific fields via field-level ACLs.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: There is a P1 incident and you want to restrict users from changing priority from P1 to P2. How will you do that?
rows.questionText: Use a Before Update Business Rule with a condition checking if priority is being changed from P1 to P2, then abort the action.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: What is an unauthorized change?
rows.answerText: An unauthorized change is a change made to the IT infrastructure without going through the formal Change Management process — no change record raised, no approval obtained. It is a violation of ITIL best practice and can be identified during audits or post-incident reviews. ServiceNow can detect these by comparing Discovery-identified CI changes against approved change records.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: Have you worked on the Change module? Why we use it? Types? What changes do we use?
rows.answerText:
Change Management is used to control the lifecycle of changes to minimize risk and disruption to IT services. Types are:

Standard — pre-approved, low-risk, routine changes (e.g., password reset). No CAB approval needed.
Normal — planned changes that go through full CAB review and approval before implementation.
Emergency — urgent changes needed to resolve a critical issue; approved by CAB-EC with expedited process and mandatory PIR after.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Based on "Requested For" value, auto-populate email, phone, location, and manager.
rows.questionText: Use an onChange Client Script on the requested_for field with GlideAjax calling a Script Include.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title:
How can you call a server-side script from the client side? Tell me all possible ways.
There are three ways:
rows.questionText:
1. GlideAjax — calls a Script Include asynchronously from a client script.
2. g_scratchpad — uses a Display Business Rule to pass data at form load time.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: What is a Business Rule and its types? Explain each of them.
rows.answerText:
A Business Rule is a server-side script that runs automatically on database operations. Its types are:

Before — runs before the record is written to the DB; changes to current are saved automatically. Used for field manipulation before save.
After — runs after the record is written; used to trigger actions based on saved data. Avoid current.update() here.
Async — runs in the background after the transaction; does not hold the form. Used for non-critical operations like notifications or creating related records.
Display — runs when a record is loaded on the form; used to pass server-side data to client scripts via g_scratchpad.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: What is multi-row variable set?
rows.answerText: A Multi-Row Variable Set (MRVS) is a type of variable set on a catalog item that allows users to add multiple rows of grouped variables — similar to a table. For example, ordering access for multiple applications at once, where each row has its own app name, access level, and justification. Each row is stored as a separate record in sc_multi_row_question_answer.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > User Criteria & Data Visibility
rows.title: What is user criteria?
rows.answerText: User Criteria is a record in ServiceNow that defines conditions to control who can view or access catalog items, knowledge articles, or content. It uses a combination of users, groups, roles, companies, and departments. Instead of hardcoding individual users, you attach user criteria to a catalog item under "Available For" or "Not Available For" to control visibility dynamicall

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is the latest version of ServiceNow release?
rows.answerText: The latest ServiceNow release is Zurich, released in Q4 2025. Cyntexa ServiceNow has also broken its city-naming tradition after exhausting the alphabet with Zurich — the next releases will be named after countries, with Australia expected in Q2 2026 and Brazil in Q4 2026.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A CI is retired but still appears in incident selection. How could this be wrong?
rows.answerText: The CI's operational status may not have been set correctly to Retired or Decommissioned — simply closing a ticket or removing it from Discovery is not enough. The CI record must have its Operational Status set to Retired and Install Status updated accordingly. A UI Policy or reference qualifier on the Incident CI field should filter out CIs with retired status from the lookup list to prevent agents from selecting them.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: CMDB Health score is low even though Discovery is successful. Why?
rows.answerText: Discovery populating CIs does not guarantee CMDB health. Low health scores can be caused by missing required attributes on CI records, stale CIs that are no longer discovered but still active, duplicate records, broken relationships between CIs, or CIs not conforming to the correct CI class. CMDB Health uses completeness, compliance, and correctness metrics — all three need to be addressed, not just CI creation.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Incidents are logged without selecting CIs. How does this impact ITSM and how would you fix it?
rows.answerText: Without CI selection, incidents cannot be linked to affected infrastructure, making impact analysis, trend reporting, and Problem Management less effective. CMDB health and service mapping also suffer. To fix this, make the CI field mandatory on the Incident form using a UI Policy when a certain category is selected. A Business Rule can also validate CI population before the record is saved for high-priority incidents.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Duplicate CIs are appearing in CMDB. How would you identify and resolve this?
rows.answerText: Use the CMDB Deduplication tool or Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE) to identify duplicate CIs based on matching rules. Review the CI Identification rules to ensure the correct unique identifiers (like serial number or hostname) are being used. Merge or retire duplicate records using the CMDB UI. Correct the Discovery or import source to prevent future duplicates by ensuring consistent identifier data is being sent.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Discovery is running but CIs are not getting created. What checks would you perform?
rows.answerText: Check the MID Server status to ensure it is up and communicating. Review Discovery Schedules to confirm they are active and targeting the correct IP ranges. Check Discovery Logs under the Discovery Status record for errors. Verify that the Probe and Sensor configuration is correct for the target device type. Confirm that the credentials used by Discovery have the required permissions on the target systems.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: SLA reports show poor performance but resolution seems fine. What could be the reasons?
rows.answerText: SLA timers may be starting late or not pausing correctly — check the Start and Pause conditions on the SLA definition. The schedule attached to the SLA may be incorrect, causing business hours to be miscalculated. Retroactive start may be misconfigured. SLA records may have been manually cancelled or reset. It is also possible that the SLA definition was recently changed and historical records reflect old targets.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A user closes incidents without adding resolution details. How would you prevent this using configuration?
rows.answerText: Use a combination of UI Policy and a Before Business Rule. The UI Policy makes Resolution Code and Resolution Notes mandatory when the state is set to Resolved. The Business Rule acts as a server-side safety net to reject the save if those fields are empty, covering cases where the UI Policy is bypassed via API or list edit.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: Multiple catalog requests are delayed due to approvals. How would you optimize the process?
rows.answerText: Review approval conditions and remove unnecessary approval steps for low-risk items. Configure auto-approval for items below a cost or risk threshold using Flow Designer conditions. Set approval timeouts with escalation so requests don't sit idle. Use group approvals instead of individual approvers to avoid single points of failure. Delegate approval authority during absences using the out-of-office delegation feature.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Knowledge articles exist but agents don't use them. How would you improve adoption?
rows.answerText: Enable the Knowledge widget on the Incident form so related articles surface automatically based on short description keywords. Configure suggested articles in the portal. Set a mandatory step in the resolution process to search knowledge before closing. Track knowledge usage in reports and incentivize agents through team metrics. Ensure articles are kept current — outdated content is a key reason agents stop trusting them.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A user wants to reopen a closed incident after 10 days. Should it be reopened or recreated?
rows.answerText: It depends on the organization's ITSM policy. Generally, if it is the same issue that was not fully resolved, reopen the existing incident to maintain continuity of the record. If the incident was genuinely resolved and the issue is new, create a new incident and link it to the original. Many organizations set a reopen window (e.g., 7–10 days) after which a new incident must be raised.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A ticket is assigned to the wrong group repeatedly. How would you fix this using configuration?
rows.answerText: Review and fix the Assignment Rules under the relevant table — check the conditions and ensure the correct group is mapped. If the issue is agents manually selecting the wrong group, a UI Policy or Client Script can be added to auto-set the group based on category or other fields. If needed, a Before Business Rule can enforce correct assignment based on defined conditions before the record is saved.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Users complain they are not getting notification emails. How do you troubleshoot without coding?
rows.answerText: Check System Mailboxes → Outbound to see if emails are being sent. Review System Notifications to confirm the notification is active and the conditions are correct. Check the Notification Log under System Log to see if the notification was triggered but failed. Verify the user's email address is populated and their notification preference is not disabled. Also check if any email filters or digest settings are suppressing delivery.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: An emergency change is requested late night. What approvals are required?
rows.answerText: An Emergency Change typically requires approval from the Change Advisory Board Emergency Committee (CAB-EC), which is a smaller group authorized to approve emergency changes quickly. In ServiceNow, the change type is set to Emergency, which triggers a separate approval flow with the CAB-EC members. A full PIR is mandatory after implementation.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: A change caused a production outage. How would you handle post-implementation review?
rows.answerText: We raise a Post Implementation Review (PIR) on the Change record, document the timeline of events, identify what went wrong during implementation, and assess the impact. A linked Problem record is created to drive root cause analysis. Remediation steps, rollback plans, and lessons learned are documented to prevent recurrence. The change process itself is also reviewed if gaps in testing or approval are identified.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: The business wants faster resolution for VIP users. How would you design this using ITSM processes?
rows.answerText: We can create a VIP user group and configure an Assignment Rule or Business Rule to automatically set priority to P1 and assign to a dedicated support group when the caller is a VIP. SLA definitions can have separate targets for VIP users using conditions. Notifications can alert senior agents immediately, and a catalog item can be created for VIP-specific requests with expedited approval.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: An incident keeps recurring every week. When do you raise a Problem record?
rows.answerText: A Problem record should be raised when a recurring incident pattern is identified and the root cause is unknown or unresolved. If the same or similar incidents are appearing repeatedly, it indicates an underlying infrastructure or configuration issue. The Problem record drives root cause analysis (RCA) and a permanent fix, and known errors are documented so agents can apply workarounds in the meantime.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A user requests new software. Why should this go through Request Fulfillment instead of Incident?
rows.answerText: Incident Management handles unplanned disruptions to normal service. A software request is a planned, expected need — not a break-fix situation. Routing it through Request Fulfillment (Service Catalog) ensures proper approval, licensing checks, procurement steps, and fulfillment tasks are followed, keeping ITSM process data clean and reportable.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: An incident is nearing SLA breach but no one is working on it. What steps would you take?
rows.answerText: First, check if an SLA breach notification or escalation rule is configured — if not, that should be fixed. Immediately reassign the incident to the correct group, notify the group manager, and update the work notes. Longer term, configure SLA breach warning notifications at 50%, 75%, and 90% elapsed time using notification rules and escalation policies so this is caught automatically in future.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Multiple users report email outage. How would you handle this as a Major Incident?
rows.answerText: We identify one incident as the Master Incident and link all related child incidents to it. We assign it as a Major Incident (P1), engage the Major Incident Manager, form a bridge call, notify stakeholders, and provide regular updates via the Major Incident Workbench. Once resolved, we trigger a Problem record for root cause analysis and document the timeline for the post-incident review.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: A user reports the same issue repeatedly. How do you decide whether to create a new Incident or link to an existing one?
rows.answerText: If the previous incident is still open or recently resolved and the root cause has not been fixed, we link the new report to the existing incident as a related record or reopen it. If the previous incident was fully resolved and the issue has now reoccurred after a period of normal operation, we create a new incident and link it to a Problem record to track the recurring root cause.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: Why should we avoid heavy scripting in Client Scripts?
rows.answerText: Client Scripts run in the browser, so heavy scripting increases page load time, causes UI lag, and degrades the user experience. Expensive operations like synchronous GlideAjax calls or large loops block the browser thread. Heavy logic should be moved to server-side Script Includes called asynchronously, keeping client scripts lightweight and responsive.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What are ACL scripts and why are they important?
rows.questionText: ACL scripts are server-side JavaScript conditions written inside an ACL rule that determine whether access should be granted. They run in addition to role and condition checks. They are important because they allow complex, dynamic access logic — for example, restricting access based on the user's department or the record's current state — that simple role checks alone cannot handle.
rows.questionCode:
// Example: Allow access only if the user is the caller or in the admin role
answer = (current.caller_id == gs.getUserID() || gs.hasRole('admin'));

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is Client–Server interaction in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: Client-side scripts (Client Scripts, UI Policies) run in the browser and handle form behavior. When they need server-side data, they communicate with the server using GlideAjax, which calls a Script Include without refreshing the page. The server processes the request and returns the result to the client. This separation ensures security — business logic stays on the server while UI logic stays on the client.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is gs.log() vs gs.info()?
rows.answerText: Both write messages to the system log. gs.log() is an older method and always writes to the log regardless of log level. gs.info() is the preferred modern method and writes at the Info log level, allowing log output to be controlled by the configured log level of the instance. In production, gs.info() is preferred for better log management.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is the role of current and previous objects?
rows.answerText: current refers to the record being acted upon in a Business Rule and reflects the latest field values being saved. previous holds the values of the record before the update was made, allowing comparison to check what changed. previous is only available in Before and After Update Business Rules.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > GlideRecord & GlideAggregate
rows.title: What is GlideRecord and what is its purpose?
rows.questionText: GlideRecord is a server-side API used to query, create, update, and delete records in ServiceNow tables. It works like a database cursor — you define a query, run it, and iterate through the results using next().

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: Difference between global Script Include and scoped Script Include.
rows.answerText: A global Script Include is accessible from anywhere in the instance across all scopes. A scoped Script Include belongs to a specific application scope and is only accessible within that scope unless explicitly marked as accessible from other scopes, providing better encapsulation and security.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Script Includes & Client-Server Communication
rows.title: What are Script Includes and why do we use them?
rows.answerText: Script Includes are reusable server-side JavaScript libraries that can be called from Business Rules, GlideAjax, REST APIs, and other server-side scripts. They promote code reusability and separation of logic, avoiding duplication across multiple scripts.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: What is a Display Business Rule and why is it used?
rows.answerText: A Display Business Rule runs when a record is loaded on the form, before it is displayed to the user. It is used to pass server-side data to client scripts using the g_scratchpad object, avoiding the need for a GlideAjax call at form load time.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Difference between Before and After Business Rule.
rows.answerText: A Before Business Rule runs before the record is saved to the database, so changes to current are saved automatically without calling current.update(). An After Business Rule runs after the record is saved, so current fields reflect the saved values but calling current.update() again can cause recursive triggers.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: What is a Business Rule and what are its types?
rows.answerText: A Business Rule is a server-side script that runs automatically when a record is inserted, updated, deleted, or displayed. Its four main types are Before (runs before DB write), After (runs after DB write), Async (runs in background after transaction), and Display (runs when record loads on form, used with g_scratchpad).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: When should you use a UI Policy instead of a Client Script?
rows.answerText: Use UI Policy for simple, no-code form behavior like making fields mandatory, read-only, or visible based on conditions — without writing scripts. Use a Client Script when complex logic, conditions, or dynamic behavior is needed that UI Policy conditions cannot handle alone.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Difference between Client Script and Business Rule.
rows.answerText: Client Script runs in the browser and controls UI behavior such as hiding fields or validating input. Business Rule runs on the server at the database level and controls data operations. Client Scripts can be bypassed if someone accesses data via API, whereas Business Rules cannot be bypassed.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is client-side scripting and where does it run?
rows.answerText: Client-side scripting runs in the user's browser and is used to control form behavior. It uses APIs like g_form, g_user, and GlideAjax. It is written in Client Scripts, UI Policies, and UI Actions. It cannot directly access the database and must use GlideAjax to fetch server-side data.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is server-side scripting in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: Server-side scripting runs on the ServiceNow server and uses the GlideSystem APIs like GlideRecord, gs, and GlideAjax. It is used in Business Rules, Script Includes, and Scheduled Jobs to interact directly with the database. It is not visible to the end user and executes securely on the server.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: For an auto-assignment scenario, where will you write this logic and why is it better than multiple assignment rules?
rows.questionText: A Before Insert/Update Business Rule on the Incident table. We check the priority value and assign the group accordingly using GlideRecord or hardcoded sys_ids via System Properties.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Incident & Problem Management
rows.title: Where will you enforce this validation to prevent users from closing incidents without filling Resolution Code and Resolution Notes?
rows.questionText: Both — Client Script for immediate UI feedback and Business Rule as a server-side safety net. Client Script (onSubmit) checks if the state is Resolved/Closed and the fields are empty, then alerts the user and returns false to stop submission. Business Rule (Before Update) acts as a backend enforcement in case the client script is bypassed.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Can we call Business Rules in Client Scripts, and how?
rows.answerText: We cannot call a Business Rule directly from a Client Script. However, we can use GlideAjax to invoke a Script Include from a client script, and that Script Include can contain server-side logic similar to what a Business Rule would do. g_scratchpad is used only with Display Business Rules to pass data to client scripts at form load — it is not a way to call a Business Rule dynamically.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > GlideRecord & GlideAggregate
rows.title: If I have a group where there are 200 members how can I remove them all?
rows.answerText: We can use GlideRecord to query the sys_user_grmember table filtered by the group sys_id and call deleteRecord() in a loop or use deleteMultiple() to remove all members at once. This can be done via a Background Script or Fix Script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What is E-Bonding integration?
rows.answerText: E-Bonding is a bidirectional integration pattern between two ServiceNow instances that keeps records continuously synchronized. When a record is created or updated in one instance, the changes are automatically pushed to the corresponding record in the other instance, and vice versa, ensuring both environments stay in sync in near real time.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What are the prerequisites required to check the feasibility of integration?
rows.answerText: We need the API endpoint URL, authentication details (credentials, OAuth tokens, or API keys), the supported protocol (REST/SOAP), firewall and network accessibility, payload format (JSON/XML), rate limits, and an understanding of the data model on both sides to map fields correctly. If integrating with on-premise systems, MID Server availability must also be confirmed.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: How can I fetch all the RITMs and variables from a catalog REQ and create an API?
rows.answerText: We can create a Scripted REST API with a GET endpoint that accepts a REQ number, queries the sc_request table to get the REQ, then queries sc_req_item for all associated RITMs using the request sys_id. For each RITM, we use GlideserviceCatalogUtil or query sc_item_option_mtom to fetch variables, and return the combined data as a JSON response.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: If I have 10 variables how can I pass them all through events in flow designer?
rows.answerText: Flow Designer does not pass variables through events directly — instead, we use data pills to carry field and variable values across steps within the flow. If using an event-triggered flow, we pass the record reference and then retrieve all required variables from the RITM or task record within the flow using Get Catalog Variables action.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: How can I cancel the execution of a flow?
rows.answerText: We can cancel a running flow from Flow Designer → Executions, find the specific flow execution, and use the Cancel option. Programmatically, we can use the FlowAPI.cancel() method by passing the flow execution sys_id to stop it from a script.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: If I want to change the SLA from 8hrs to 4hrs how to do it if it is already in production?
rows.answerText: Make the change to the SLA Definition in a non-production instance, capture it in an Update Set, and move it to production during a maintenance window such as a weekend to avoid disruption to active SLAs. Existing in-progress SLA records may need to be reviewed separately as they may not automatically reflect the updated duration.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Catalog Items & Variables
rows.title: Can we add a knowledge article in the catalog?
rows.answerText: Yes, we can link a Knowledge article to a catalog item by enabling the Knowledge field on the catalog item and associating the relevant article. This allows users submitting the catalog item to see related knowledge articles that may resolve their request before submission.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How can I create an incident to cancel another incident?
rows.answerText: We can add a custom Reference field on the Incident form pointing to the Incident table to capture the incident to be cancelled. Then use an Async Business Rule that triggers on insert/update of the new incident, reads the referenced incident using GlideRecord, and sets its state to Cancelled.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: If a catalog request is raised by mistake how can we cancel it?
rows.answerText: We can cancel the REQ and its associated RITMs by opening the Request record and setting the state to Cancelled, provided the request has not already been fulfilled. If the flow or workflow is already running, it needs to be cancelled separately from the flow execution context or workflow context before closing the records.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: Have you worked on upgrades?
rows.answerText: During upgrades, the instance is upgraded to a new ServiceNow release, and customizations are flagged as skipped if they conflict with baseline changes. The process involves reviewing the upgrade monitor, resolving skipped records by merging customizations with the new baseline, and regression testing to ensure existing functionality is intact.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Client Scripts & UI Policies
rows.title: What is the purpose of the "Isolate Script" checkbox in Client Scripts?
rows.answerText: ServiceNow discourages direct DOM manipulation as it can break after upgrades. The Isolate Script checkbox ensures the client script runs in an isolated scope, preventing access to the DOM and enforcing the use of ServiceNow's standard client-side APIs like g_form and g_user only.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How will you setup OAuth 2.0 authentication?
rows.answerText: We create an OAuth Provider record under System OAuth → Application Registry with the client ID, client secret, token URL, and authorization URL. Then in the REST Message, we set the authentication type to OAuth 2.0 and reference that provider profile. ServiceNow handles token retrieval and refresh automatically from that point.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you test integrations in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: We can test using the Test button available in the REST Message function record, which sends a real request and shows the response. We verify the HTTP status code (200/201 for success), check the response body, and review logs in System Logs → Application Logs. For inbound APIs, tools like Postman can be used to send test payloads to the ServiceNow endpoint.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: How do you design a scalable approval architecture?
rows.answerText: We can use Flow Designer with dynamic approval steps where approvers are determined by group, role, or a custom script rather than hardcoded users. For multi-level approvals, we chain Ask for Approval steps with conditions. Using approval policies and delegation rules ensures the architecture scales without needing to modify flows when team structures change.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you handle bulk data transfer?
rows.answerText: We use Import Sets and Transform Maps to handle bulk data transfer. Data is uploaded into a staging (import set) table via file upload or a scheduled import source, and the Transform Map then maps and inserts or updates the records into the target table. For large volumes, scheduled imports or the Integration Hub can be used to automate and manage the process.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: How does ACL evaluation work in API calls?
rows.answerText: When an API call is made to ServiceNow, ACLs are evaluated against the user account making the request, the same way they are for UI access. If a table-level or field-level ACL denies access to the authenticating user, the API will either return a 403 error or omit the restricted fields from the response. Roles, conditions, and scripts defined in the ACL are all evaluated during the API request.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: When do you use orderBy() vs .sort()?
rows.answerText: orderBy() is a GlideRecord server-side method used to sort database query results before they are returned from ServiceNow — it sorts at the database level. .sort() is a JavaScript array method used to sort data that is already retrieved and stored in an array in memory. Use orderBy() when querying records, and .sort() when sorting a JavaScript array after data has already been fetched.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you implement a retry mechanism?
rows.answerText: We can implement a retry mechanism by wrapping the REST call in a loop with a maximum retry count, checking the response status code after each attempt, and pausing between retries using a counter or scheduled logic. For async scenarios, we can use Flow Designer with error handling steps or a scheduled job that retries failed records flagged in a custom table.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you avoid hardcoding credentials?
rows.answerText: We use ServiceNow's Connection & Credential Aliases to store credentials securely. In scripts, we reference the alias instead of hardcoding usernames or passwords. System Properties can also be used for non-sensitive configuration values that may change across environments.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you secure outbound REST calls?
rows.answerText: We secure outbound REST calls by using HTTPS endpoints, configuring authentication (Basic, OAuth, or API Key) in the REST Message record, storing credentials in Connection & Credential aliases instead of hardcoding them, and restricting REST Message records using roles so only authorized users can modify them.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you handle error logging in REST integration?
rows.answerText: We use try-catch blocks around the REST call and log errors using gs.error() or gs.warn(). We can also check the HTTP response status code and log the response body if the call fails. Logs can be reviewed in System Logs → Application Logs. For outbound REST Messages, the ECC Queue and REST Message logs can also be used for troubleshooting.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you design an integration between two ServiceNow instances?
rows.answerText: We use e-Bonding, which is a bidirectional integration pattern between two ServiceNow instances. It typically involves outbound REST Messages or IntegrationHub spokes on one instance calling the Table API or Scripted REST API of the other instance. Business Rules or Flows trigger the outbound call when a record is created or updated, and the receiving instance processes the payload accordingly.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: How do you calculate risk in Change Management?
rows.answerText: Risk in Change Management is calculated based on factors like the number of impacted CIs, the criticality of those CIs, the change type, the environment affected, and historical failure rates. ServiceNow also provides a Risk Assessment questionnaire that calculates a risk score automatically based on answers provided during change creation.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Approvals & Approval Workflows
rows.title: What happens when one approver rejects?
rows.answerText: It depends on the approval rule configured. If the rule is set to "Everyone must approve," then a single rejection will reject the entire approval. If the rule is "Anyone can approve," a rejection by one approver does not reject the request as long as at least one other approver approves it.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: What is the difference between Workflow and Flow Designer?
rows.answerText: Both are used to automate step-by-step processes on records or catalog items based on conditions. Workflow is the older engine, is more complex, and often requires scripting. Flow Designer is the modern replacement, is low-code/no-code, more user-friendly, supports data pills for passing data between steps, and integrates natively with IntegrationHub. Workflow is still supported but Flow Designer is the recommended approach for new development.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Change Management
rows.title: How do you auto-approve low-risk changes?
rows.answerText: We can use Flow Designer or a Business Rule to check if the change risk is low, and if so, automatically set the approval state to Approved and move the change to the next state, bypassing the manual approval step. This can also be achieved using Change Approval Policies in the Change Management module.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: How do you configure approvals in Flow Designer?
rows.answerText: In Flow Designer, we add the Ask for Approval action step, configure the table and record to approve, define the approvers (by user, group, or dynamic value), and set the approval rule such as anyone approves or everyone must approve. The flow then branches based on the approval outcome — Approved or Rejected.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is the difference between execute() and executeAsync()?
rows.answerText: execute() sends the REST request synchronously and waits for the response before continuing script execution. executeAsync() sends the request asynchronously in the background without waiting for the response, which is useful for non-critical outbound calls where you don't need to process the response immediately.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What happens if an ACL denies access through an API?
rows.answerText: If an ACL denies access, the API will return a 403 Forbidden response for that record or field. The external system will not be able to read or modify the restricted data, and in some cases the field will simply be omitted from the response without an explicit error.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you configure Basic Authentication in a REST Message?
rows.answerText: In the REST Message record, navigate to the Authentication tab, set the Authentication Type to Basic, and provide the username and password. These credentials are then automatically encoded and sent in the Authorization header with each outbound request.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: How do you call another ServiceNow instance from a server-side script?
rows.answerText: We can use the RESTMessageV2 API in a server-side script to make HTTP calls to another ServiceNow instance. We define the endpoint URL of the target instance, set authentication credentials, add headers, and use .execute() to send the request and retrieve the response.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What is the difference between Table API and Scripted REST API?
rows.answerText: Table API is an out-of-the-box API provided by ServiceNow to perform standard CRUD operations on any table without any custom development. Scripted REST API is a custom API built by developers when specific business logic, custom endpoints, or a tailored response format is needed that the Table API cannot provide out of the box.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What is Table API?
rows.answerText: Table API is a REST-based API provided by ServiceNow that allows external systems or scripts to perform CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) on any ServiceNow table using standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What are function parameters (a, b)?
rows.answerText: Parameters are placeholder variables defined in a function signature that accept values (arguments) passed when the function is called. They can be used any number of times inside the function. Once the logic is complete, the result can be returned to the caller using the return keyword. For example, function add(a, b) { return a + b; } — here a and b are parameters.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: How does && (logical AND) work?
rows.answerText: && evaluates two conditions and returns true only if both conditions are true. If the first condition is false, it short-circuits and does not evaluate the second condition. For example, if (a > 0 && b > 0) executes only when both a and b are greater than zero.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is the difference between push() and pop()?
rows.answerText: push() adds one or more elements to the end of an array and returns the new length. pop() removes the last element from an array and returns that removed element.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: What is .shift()?
rows.answerText: .shift() removes the first element from an array and returns that removed element, reducing the array length by one. It is the opposite of .unshift(), which adds elements to the beginning of an array.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: Why does .sort() not give correct numeric sorting?
rows.answerText: Because by default .sort() converts elements to strings and compares them lexicographically. So numbers like [10, 2, 1] would sort as [1, 10, 2] instead of [1, 2, 10]. To sort numerically, a comparator function must be passed: array.sort((a, b) => a - b).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Core JavaScript & Scripting Fundamentals
rows.title: How does .sort() work in JavaScript?
rows.answerText: .sort() sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the sorted array. By default, it converts elements to strings and sorts them in ascending alphabetical (Unicode) order. A custom comparator function can be passed to define custom sort logic, such as numeric sorting.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: What is coalesce and can we make more than one field as coalesce true?
rows.answerText: Coalesce is used in a Transform Map to designate a field as a unique identifier — if a matching record is found based on that field, it updates the existing record instead of creating a duplicate. Yes, we can set more than one field as coalesce true, in which case ServiceNow will use a combination of all coalesced fields to find a matching record.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: Explain the types of transform map scripts with a scenario.
rows.answerText: Transform Map scripts are: onBefore (runs before a row is transformed — used to validate or manipulate source data), onAfter (runs after a row is transformed — used to perform actions on the created/updated record), onComplete (runs after all rows are processed — used for summary actions), and onReject (runs when a row is rejected). For example, if importing user data, an onBefore script can check if the email field is empty and skip that row, while an onAfter script can assign a role to the newly created user.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Data Management > Import Sets & Transform Maps
rows.title: What are transform maps?
rows.answerText: A Transform Map defines how data from an import set (staging table) maps to a target table in ServiceNow. It is used to load bulk data into a table by mapping source columns to destination fields, instead of creating records manually one by one.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What common challenges do you face when setting up integrations with ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: Common challenges include firewall ports being blocked, incorrect or expired credentials, insufficient permissions on the external system, SSL/certificate issues, payload format mismatches (JSON/XML), and MID Server connectivity issues when integrating with on-premise systems.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Integrations & APIs > REST APIs & Table API
rows.title: What are the primary use cases for a Mid Server?
rows.answerText: The MID Server is a Java-based application that establishes secure communication between ServiceNow and external environments. Primary use cases include Discovery, Orchestration, ITOM integrations, connecting to on-premise systems behind firewalls, and importing data from external sources that cannot directly reach the ServiceNow instance.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: How do you use the ACL debug functionality?
rows.answerText: We can enable ACL debugging by navigating to System Diagnostics → Session Debug → Debug Security. Then impersonate the user in question, navigate to the record or form, and the debug output will show which ACLs are being evaluated, whether they passed or failed, and why — helping identify access issues.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: What is the purpose of the "Cascade variables" checkbox in an Order Guide?
rows.answerText: The "Cascade variables" checkbox in an Order Guide allows variables defined at the Order Guide level to be automatically passed down and mapped to the variables of the individual catalog items included in it, so users don't have to fill in the same information multiple times.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: Explain the "3-record structure" (Request, Request Item, Task) created when a catalog item is submitted.
rows.answerText: When a catalog item is submitted, a Request (REQ) is created as the top-level order. Each catalog item within that request gets its own Request Item (RITM). Each RITM can have one or more Service Catalog Tasks (SCTASK) created for fulfillment, depending on the workflow or flow configured. For example, ordering from Amazon with 5 items gives one order number (REQ), each item has its own tracking number (RITM), and each item may have fulfillment steps (SCTASK).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > Flow Designer
rows.title: What are "record pills" or "data pills" in Flow Designer?
rows.answerText: Data pills are references to data from a previous step or trigger in a Flow Designer flow. They carry field values from a record and can be reused across any subsequent steps in the same flow. For example, if a flow is triggered on an Incident, the incident's fields like number, caller, or priority are available as data pills throughout the entire flow.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How do you debug a Business Rule?
rows.answerText: We can use gs.info(), gs.warn(), or gs.error() to log messages, which can then be viewed in System Logs → Application Logs. We cannot use alert() since Business Rules are server-side. We can also use the Script Debugger available under System Diagnostics for step-through debugging.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: What are the advantages of an Async Business Rule over an After Business Rule, and vice versa?
rows.answerText: Async BR runs in the background without holding the form, making it better for performance and non-critical operations like sending notifications or creating related records. After BR ensures the logic executes in the same transaction, making it better when data integrity is required and the operation must complete before the user is released from the save action.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Scheduled Jobs & Background Scripts
rows.title: What is the difference between a fix script and a background script?
rows.answerText: A Fix Script is stored in the database, can be added to an update set, and can be reused or promoted across instances. A Background Script is used for one-time ad hoc execution, is not stored, cannot be added to an update set, and is mainly used for testing or quick data operations in a single session.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: When should you avoid using an Asynchronous Business Rule?
rows.answerText: Avoid Async Business Rules when data integrity is critical — since Async runs in the background after the transaction completes, it cannot roll back if the main transaction fails. If the logic must succeed before proceeding or if you need guaranteed execution in sync with the save operation, use a Before or After Business Rule instead.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Explain a scenario where you would use a Display Business Rule instead of GlideAjax.
rows.answerText: A Display Business Rule is used when you want to pass server-side data to a client script using g_scratchpad before the form loads — for example, passing a field value or a flag to control UI behavior on load. GlideAjax is used when you need to fetch server-side data dynamically after the form has already loaded, such as on a field change event. Use Display BR when the data is needed at form load time without an extra round trip.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How do you prevent Business Rules and Workflows from executing?
rows.answerText: For Business Rules, we can set them as inactive or add a condition so they don't meet the execution criteria. We can also use current.setAbortAction(true) inside the script. For Workflows, we can inactivate the workflow version or use workflow conditions to prevent it from triggering.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: What are Retroactive Start and Retroactive Pause in SLA?
rows.answerText: Retroactive Start means the SLA timer starts from the time the record was originally created, regardless of when the SLA condition was actually met. Retroactive Pause means the pause duration is calculated from the beginning of the record's creation, so any time the ticket was in a paused state — even before the SLA attached — is accounted for and subtracted from the elapsed time.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What is an Access Control List (ACL)?
rows.answerText: An ACL is a security feature in ServiceNow that controls access to data at two levels — row level (configured as table.None) to restrict access to entire records, and field level (configured as table.field_name) to restrict access to specific fields. ACLs can be controlled using roles, conditions, and scripts.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: Should I use current.update() in an After Update Business Rule?
rows.answerText: No. An After Business Rule executes after the record has already been saved to the database. Calling current.update() again would trigger another database save, which could cause infinite loops or unintentionally re-trigger other business rules and scripts.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: How do you prevent a script from executing?
rows.answerText: There are a few ways: we can set the script's Active field to false to disable it entirely. We can also add a condition within the script logic to control when it should not execute. Additionally, in Business Rules, we can use current.setAbortAction(true) to abort the action when a specific condition is met.
