rows.title: What is the use of GlideAjax and can you explain with a real-time example where you have used it?
rows.answerText: GlideAjax is a client-side API that allows you to call a server-side Script Include from a client script to retrieve or process data without refreshing the form. For example, when a caller is selected on the Incident form, GlideAjax can be used to fetch and auto-populate that user's email and department fields in real time by invoking a Script Include that queries the User table.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: What is an SLA in ServiceNow, and how do you create and configure it?
rows.answerText: SLA stands for Service Level Agreement, which is a contract between a service provider and a client defining the expected service standards and response/resolution times. In ServiceNow, SLAs are configured under Service Level Management → SLA Definitions, where you define the name, target table, duration, schedule, start, pause, stop, and reset conditions.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Scripting & Automation > Business Rules
rows.title: What is a Business Rule, what are its types briefly, and how does it execute?
rows.answerText: Rule is a server-side script that executes at the database level in ServiceNow. Its four major types are: Before (runs before the record is written to the database), After (runs after the record is written), Async (runs in the background after the transaction is complete without holding the form), and Display (runs when a record is loaded on the form, used to pass data to client scripts via g_scratchpad).

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: Scenario: I want to restrict access to three specific fields on the Incident table for a particular user group using ACLs; how will you achieve this and explain step by step?
rows.answerText: To restrict access to three specific fields on the Incident table for a user group, I would create field-level ACLs in ServiceNow — one ACL per field, so three ACLs total. For each ACL, I'd select the Incident table, pick the specific field, set the operation to read or write depending on whether I want to restrict visibility or editing. Then in the script condition, I'd use gs.getUser().isMemberOf('Group Name') and negate it — so the ACL passes for everyone except that group. Finally, I'd test it using ACL debug mode with a user from that group to confirm the fields are restricted. Each field requires its own ACL because ACLs in ServiceNow are granular — table-level and field-level rules are separate.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Workflow & Flow Designer > SLA Management
rows.title: What do you mean by Retroactive Start and Retroactive Stop in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: Retroactive Start means the SLA timer begins from the time the record was created, not from when the SLA condition was first met. There is no "Retroactive Stop" in ServiceNow — instead, we have a Pause condition, which when configured retroactively, calculates and subtracts the pause duration from the very beginning of the record's creation.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What is the difference between .none and .* ACLs?
rows.answerText:
Table.none is a record-level ACL — it controls access to the entire record, so things like whether a user can read, create, write, or delete it.
Table.* is a field-level wildcard — it applies to all fields in that table at once. So instead of setting ACLs on each field individually, you can use Table.* to cover all of them in one go.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Security & ACLs > ACLs & Roles
rows.title: What is an ACL in ServiceNow?
rows.answerText: ACL stands for Access Control List. It helps us control who can access what in ServiceNow — we can restrict access at the table level, field level, or record level based on conditions we define. It's basically how we manage security and make sure users only see and interact with what they're supposed to.

rows.nodePath: ServiceNow > ITSM > Service Catalog > Order Guides & Request Fulfillment
rows.title: How to close REQ and RITM automatically when the task is closed?
rows.questionText:
There are two ways to handle this. One is using a business rule on the SC Task table, where we set the condition to trigger when the task state is closed and then update the RITM and REQ state accordingly.
The preferred approach, however, is Flow Designer. We create a flow triggered by the SC Task record, add a condition for when the task is closed, and then use Update Record actions to close the RITM and REQ. It's easier to read, troubleshoot, and migrate compared to a business rule.
